summary: This PIMCO investor education article (June 2023) explains the basics of bonds: they are loans issued by companies, states or governments that pay periodic coupons and return principal at maturity. It covers how interest rates drive bond prices, the difference between yield and interest rate, total return, bond market types and size, yield curve shapes, and the role of bonds in diversified portfolios including duration risk. A glossary of key terms closes the note, and much of the page is site navigation and office listings that were ignored.
one_line: PIMCO's June 2023 primer on how bonds work, interest rate and price links, yield curves, duration, and bonds' role in portfolios.
key_facts: Bonds are basically loans; a company, state or government issues bonds to raise money.
The amount given to the issuer is called the principal or face value of the bond.
If a bond has a face value of $1,000 and a coupon rate of 5%, it pays total coupons of $50 per year (assumes annual payment).
If interest rates rise, older bonds with lower rates will drop in price to compensate for the lower coupon payments.
The total return of a bond has two components: the price of the bond and the coupon income or yield.
At $49 trillion, the US bond market is only slightly smaller than the US stock market.
At $127 trillion, the global bond market is larger than the global stock market.
A Normal Yield Curve is seen during typical periods of economic expansion and goes up from left to right.
An Inverted Yield Curve is seen during times of anticipated economic slowdown and in the past has been rare.
A Flat Yield Curve may be seen when the economy is in transition from expansion to slowdown or vice versa.
Duration (measured in years) estimates the % change in a bond's price for a 1% change in yield.
Bonds may help diversify a portfolio of riskier assets like equities due to the low to negative correlation of bonds with other asset classes.
Spread is the risk premium that investors demand, over a base government bond yield, to compensate for the risk taken.
Yield is the annual income that an investor earns on an investment; yields tend to be higher for longer-maturity bonds.
Unlike stocks, bonds issued by companies do not generally give investors ownership rights.
